package.name: CommandLine
package.description: Declarative command-line parsing: options, positional arguments, subcommands and generated help

modules.name: Error
modules.header:
Why arguments did not match a command, said in the terms the person who typed them will recognize.
Each case carries what it needs to be described on its own: the argument as it was typed, or the name of the option
or positional the specification gave it, so that printing an error needs neither the specification nor the
arguments. The descriptions are lower case and unpunctuated, ready to follow a program's own prefix such as
`error: `.

modules.name: Help
modules.header:
Help, usage and version text, written from the same description the arguments are checked against.
The layout is the conventional one: the summary, a usage line, then the arguments, options and subcommands, each in
two columns with the descriptions aligned. `--help` and `--version` are listed with the options a command declares,
unless it declares its own of the same name.

modules.name: Parsed
modules.header:
Arguments checked against a command, and the questions a program asks of them.
A parse holds the command, where the arguments come from and which of them belong to it, and nothing else. Each
question walks those arguments again with the scanner that validated them, so asking costs time proportional to the
number of arguments and no storage at all. Every view a question returns borrows the arguments, which outlive the
parse.
When a command has subcommands, the parse covers the arguments up to the subcommand's name and `Subcommand` gives
the parse of the rest, which was validated with the first.

modules.name: Scan
modules.header:
The one walk over arguments that parsing and every query share.
Validating once and then answering each question by walking the arguments again keeps a parse free of storage: the
walk is the record. Because both use this scanner, a question can never be answered from a reading of the
arguments different from the one that was validated.
The grammar is the conventional one. `--name` and `--name=value` are long options, and a long option that takes a
value may have it as the next argument. `-abc` is the short options `a`, `b` and `c`, and the first of them that
takes a value takes the rest of the cluster, or the next argument when it ends the cluster. `--` ends options, after
which every argument is positional, and `-` alone is positional. In a command with subcommands, the first positional
argument names the subcommand, and every argument after it belongs to the subcommand.

modules.name: Spec
modules.header:
What a command accepts, described as values rather than discovered from code.
A command is its name, a one-line summary, an optional version, its options, its positional arguments and its
subcommands. Every part is a plain value holding borrowed text and borrowed slices, so a whole command line can be
described in constants or locals and nothing is allocated. The descriptions are what parsing checks the arguments
against and what the help text is written from, so the two cannot disagree.
`--help` and `-h` are understood by every command, and `--version` and `-V` by every command that has a version,
unless the command declares an option with the same name, which then takes precedence.

doc.summary: Why the arguments did not match the command.
doc.markdown:
Why the arguments did not match the command.
Failure-only: a parse is the success channel of `Parsed ! CommandLineError`. Copy; every view and name it carries
borrows the arguments or the specification, which must outlive it.

cases.name: UnknownOption
cases.doc: An argument that looks like an option names none the command has. Carries the argument as typed.

cases.name: MissingValue
cases.doc:
An option that takes a value was the last argument, or ended a cluster of short options. Carries the option's
long name.

cases.name: UnexpectedValue
cases.doc: A flag was given a value with `=`. Carries the option's long name.

cases.name: UnknownCommand
cases.doc: The command has subcommands and the word naming one is not among them. Carries the word as typed.

cases.name: MissingCommand
cases.doc: The command has subcommands and none was named.

cases.name: MissingPositional
cases.doc: A required positional argument was not given. Carries its name.

cases.name: UnexpectedArgument
cases.doc: A positional argument beyond every one the command accepts. Carries the argument as typed.

cases.name: InvalidValue
cases.doc:
A value that could not be read as what was asked of it, such as a number. Carries the option or positional's
name, then the value as typed.

items.name: Parse
items.signature: pub func Parse(spec: *CommandSpec, arguments: OsStringView[..]) -> Parsed ! CommandLineError

doc.summary: Checks `arguments` against `spec`.
doc.markdown:
Checks `arguments` against `spec`.
`arguments` are the arguments after the program's name. Reports the first mismatch: an unknown option, an option
missing its value or given one it does not take, an unknown or missing subcommand, a missing required positional,
or an argument beyond what the command accepts. Asking for `--help` or `--version` succeeds whatever else is
missing, and `HelpRequested` or `VersionRequested` then says so. Allocates nothing; both `spec` and `arguments`
must outlive the result.

params.name: spec
params.markdown: the command the arguments are for

params.name: arguments
params.markdown: the arguments, without the program's name

doc.returns: the parse, or why the arguments do not match

doc.summary: Checks the process's own arguments against `spec`.
doc.markdown:
Checks the process's own arguments against `spec`.
The same checks as `Parse`, over every argument after the program's name. The arguments last as long as the
process; `spec` must outlive the result.

params.name: spec
params.markdown: the command the arguments are for

doc.returns: the parse, or why the arguments do not match
